title_en: Who Causes Stock Market Anomalies? (w/ Victor Haghani) | #429
title_zh: 谁造成了股市异象？对话 Victor Haghani | #429
subtitle_zh: Victor Haghani 拆解外推型投资者（extrapolators）如何制造市场异象，以及杠杆、税损收割值不值。
summary_zh: 本期 Rational Reminder（第429期）由 Ben Felix 与 Cameron Passmore 对话 Elm Wealth 创始人、Long-Term Capital Management 创始合伙人 Victor Haghani（第二次做客，上次为第270期）。核心是即将发表于 Journal of Investment Management 的论文《Who Killed the Random Walk?》。Haghani 试图用一个综合模型解释股市最顽固的异象：超额波动性（excess volatility）、水平动量、随机却持续的波动率、肥尾（fat tails）与繁荣崩溃。他们引入六七种不同类型投资者——理性价值型、价值加动量型、逢低买入的短期反转型、更具前瞻性的投资者，尤其是外推型投资者（extrapolators）——说明这些异象并非市场失灵，而是异质参与者相互作用的产物，也让人对市场能做什么多一份谦卑。节目还延伸讨论杠杆何时合理：以 Merton share 与 Kelly 公式思考仓位规模，为何边际风险调整后回报总低于预期回报，以及税损收割、杠杆 ETF 与波动率目标（vol targeting）策略。Haghani 还预告了2027年初出版的新书《Get Rich Once》。是一集兼具学术深度与实操智慧的对话。

turns.en: Understanding these extrapolators and how much they can affect behavior creates a lot more humility in terms of what the markets can and might do.
turns.zh: 理解这些外推型投资者（extrapolators）能在多大程度上影响行为，会让我们对市场能够做什么、可能会做什么，多一份谦卑。

turns.en: It's this more gradual thing. Momentum is a binary. With return chasing, it's this more gradual thing. I think as an investor, you just don't need to be following the news very much at all.
turns.zh: 它是那种更渐进的过程。动量（momentum）是个二元信号。而追逐收益（return chasing）则是个更渐进的东西。我觉得作为一个投资者，你根本不太需要去盯新闻。

turns.en: Welcome to episode 429 of the Ratchet Reminder podcast. I'm Ben Felix, Chief Investment Officer at PWL Capital. And I'm Cameron Passmore, Chief Executive Officer of PWL Capital.
turns.zh: 欢迎收听 Rational Reminder 播客第 429 期。我是 Ben Felix，PWL Capital 的首席投资官。我是 Cameron Passmore，PWL Capital 的首席执行官。

turns.en: And today, Ben, we're joined by Victor Hegani, who previously appeared in episode 270. Victor is the founder of Elm Wealth, which is a wealth advisory firm in the U.S., and he has over 40 years experience studying financial markets.
turns.zh: 今天，Ben，和我们同台的是 Victor Haghani，他上次来是第 270 期。Victor 是 Elm Wealth 的创始人，那是一家美国的财富顾问公司，他研究金融市场已经超过 40 年。

turns.en: Studying and working in them, and he's got real practical experience, too. In the episode, we discuss how different types of investors impact the market, when leverage does or does not make sense, and what financial advice Victor would give his younger self.
turns.zh: 不仅研究，也在这个市场里工作过，他有实打实的实操经验。本期我们会讨论不同类型的投资者如何影响市场，杠杆什么时候合理、什么时候不合理，以及 Victor 会给年轻时的自己什么理财建议。

turns.en: And of course, we'll talk about our thoughts of the conversation at the end. But for now, let's get to the episode with Victor. Victor Hegani, welcome back to the Ratchet Reminder podcast.
turns.zh: 当然，结尾我们也会聊聊对这期对话的看法。不过现在，先进入正题，和 Victor 的对谈。Victor Haghani，欢迎回到 Rational Reminder 播客。

turns.en: Thank you. Great to be here for a second time. I'm honored. We're excited to have you back, and we have a lot to talk about. You've been busy writing about stuff since the last time.
turns.zh: 谢谢。很高兴第二次来这里，很荣幸。我们也很高兴你回来，有好多东西可以聊。上次之后你一直没闲着，写了不少东西。

turns.en: Yes, just a little bit. So Victor, since the last time you were on, when we talked about your, at the time, new book, Missing Billionaires, what have you learned since then?
turns.zh: 对，就写了一点点。那么 Victor，自打你上次来做客、我们聊了你当时刚出版的新书《Missing Billionaires》之后，你又学到了什么？

turns.en: In some ways, the thing that we learned is that there was a gap in the literature for this kind of book with this kind of treatment. Our publisher, God Bless Them, were like, you guys have way too many equations in there.
turns.zh: 某种程度上，我们学到的是：文献里其实缺这样一本书、缺这种处理方式。我们的出版商，上帝保佑他们，当时说你们书里方程也太多了。

turns.en: You're not going to sell any books, and we're like, well, they're not hard equations. People will get them. And, you know, we've really been so pleasantly surprised by the fact that a lot of people have been interested in the book.
turns.zh: 这样卖不掉书的。我们说，这些方程不难，大家能看懂。结果真的特别惊喜，这么多人对这本书感兴趣。

turns.en: When you write about something where people have a little bit of a blank area in their minds talking about sizing and Kelly and the Merton share and all this, it's much easier to convince people because you're not changing anybody's mind.
turns.zh: 当你写的东西恰好是读者脑子里一片空白的领域——比如仓位规模（sizing）、Kelly 公式、Merton share 这些——说服人就容易多了，因为你并没有改变任何人的既有观念。

turns.en: You're just sharing with them things that they might not have known. And to be clear, we didn't come up with anything original in the Missing Billionaires.
turns.zh: 你只是在跟他们分享他们可能不知道的东西。说清楚一点：《Missing Billionaires》里我们没有发明任何原创的东西。

turns.en: We were just channeling a lot of great research of other people. So yeah, it's been satisfying for us. Another thing that we learned is that a lot of people said to us, we love this kind of treatment and this kind of discussion at this level.
turns.zh: 我们只是转述了很多别人做的了不起的研究。所以，是的，这本书对我们来说很满足。我们还学到的一点是，很多人跟我们说：我喜欢这种处理、这种深度的讨论。

turns.en: And I wish that you would write something for my kids, you know, or for my nieces or nephews or my young friends or whatever that's shorter, that doesn't go into as much depth on sizing and is it more broader things?
turns.zh: 我真希望你们能为我的孩子写点什么，或者为我侄女、侄子、年轻的朋友们写个更短的，不用在仓位规模上钻那么深、讲更宽泛一些的东西。

turns.en: So you know, as we talked about before, we wrote a book over the summer that's coming out in early 2027 called Get Rich Once and Other Financial Wisdom for Our Younger Selves.
turns.zh: 所以，就像我们之前提过的，我们夏天写了一本书，2027 年初出版，叫 Get Rich Once and Other Financial Wisdom for Our Younger Selves。

turns.en: It's going to be available on Amazon for pre-order. So we could talk about that later, but just a quick plug there. Yeah, I know that that's exciting.
turns.zh: 在 Amazon 上已经可以预售了。这个我们后面可以再聊，先简单打个广告。是啊，我知道那很让人兴奋。

turns.en: We will bring that back up later. You mentioned you didn't come up with the ideas in the book, but it's pretty rare. I don't know if I can say that you were the first, but certainly one of the first to communicate those ideas, which can be pretty mathy and pretty technical in a way that's pretty practically accessible to a broad audience.
turns.zh: 我们后面会再把它捡起来。你说书里的想法不是你们原创的，但这其实很少见。我不知道能不能说你们是第一个，但肯定是最早把那些相当数学化、相当技术性的想法，用大众在实操上能听懂的方式讲出来的之一。

turns.en: That's what you guys really brought to the table with that book. Thank you. Yeah. That's really great to hear that. I said you've been busy.
turns.zh: 那正是你们这本书带来的真正价值。谢谢。是啊。听到这话真高兴。我说你一直闲不住吧。

turns.en: You've got a paper coming out shortly in the Journal of Investment Management, Who Killed the Random Walk? So I want to ask a little bit about that.
turns.zh: 你马上要在 Journal of Investment Management 上发表一篇论文，Who Killed the Random Walk? 所以我想问问这篇论文。

turns.en: Can you talk about what some of the most persistent puzzles and stock returns are? Every class in asset pricing theory really starts off with all the things that asset pricing theory really has a tough time explaining.
turns.zh: 能讲讲股市回报里那些最顽固的谜题（puzzles）有哪些吗？每门资产定价课，开头讲的都是资产定价理论最难解释的那些东西。

turns.en: I think the biggest of all of the strange things about the stock market is this idea that there's excess volatility, that stocks bounce around by much more than fundamentals would seem to dictate.
turns.zh: 我觉得股市最反常的一点是超额波动性（excess volatility）：股价的上下波动，远远超过了基本面所能解释的范围。

turns.en: This goes back to Campbell and Schiller in the 80s and was one of the big contributions of Schiller that probably led to his Nobel Prize is this idea that stocks are so much more volatile than changes in expected earnings.
turns.zh: 这个想法可以追溯到 1980 年代 Campbell 和 Shiller 的工作，而 Shiller 大概率因此拿下诺贝尔奖的核心贡献，就是股价的波动远大于预期盈利变化的幅度。

turns.en: But there are all these other things too out there. There's persistent price level momentum in stocks. There's very stochastic volatility, but that it also persists.
turns.zh: 但外面还有好多别的东西：股价里有持续的水平动量；波动率非常随机，但它本身又具有持续性。

turns.en: There's fat tails. There's booms and busts. All of these anomalies, really each one of them, you could come up with some explanation, maybe a rational expectations type of explanation or that there's some dark matter that's doing something.
turns.zh: 还有肥尾（fat tails），有繁荣与崩溃（boom and bust）。所有这些异象（anomalies），每一个其实你都能编出一个解释，要么用理性预期的说法，要么说有什么暗物质在起作用。

turns.en: It's not that these haven't been explained, but we got attracted to trying to put together an explanation that would be comprehensive and touch on all of these.
turns.zh: 并不是说这些没人解释过，而是我们被吸引去做的是：把这些东西拼成一个能覆盖所有这些现象的、综合性的解释。

turns.en: As with the missing billionaires, it's not like we came up with anything original, but I think that maybe we took the existing research, took it one step further and also maybe posited in a way that's much easier for a broader audience to understand versus some of the more technical academic treatments that we've had.
turns.zh: 和《Missing Billionaires》一样，我们没有什么原创的东西，但我想我们可能把既有研究往前推了一步，而且我们陈述的方式让更广泛的读者更容易理解，而不像那些技术性很强的学术论述。

turns.en: How do the types of investors that participate in the market interact with the observed anomalies? Historically, the idea has been that we have this rational investor that's always looking at the long-term expected return or some expected return of what they're investing in based on cash flows.
turns.zh: 市场上参与的不同类型投资者，和这些被观察到的异象之间是怎么相互作用的？历史上，大家的想法是我们有一个理性投资者，永远在根据现金流，看长期预期回报或者某种预期回报来做投资。

turns.en: Some kind of a value investor representative agent. If that's what we had, if that's actually how investors were, then we just wouldn't see any of these anomalies.
turns.zh: 某种价值型投资者作为代表性代理人（representative agent）。如果市场真是那样，如果投资者真是那样，我们就根本不会看到这些异象。

turns.en: In fact, instead of seeing stock market volatility higher than fundamentals, we would actually see these fundamental value investors dampening volatility because when the market would go down and expected returns would be higher, they would want to own a little bit more than what they owned because now what they owned was worth less because prices had gone down.
turns.zh: 事实上，我们看到的股市波动不会高于基本面，反而会看到那些基本面价值型投资者在压低波动：因为市场跌下去、预期回报变高时，他们会想多持有一点——尽管他们手上东西因为价格下跌已经贬值了。

turns.en: They would be dampening volatility a little bit, but instead we actually see volatility exacerbated by different investor types. In the simplest form of our model, we have three investor types.
turns.zh: 他们会略微压低波动，但实际我们看到的是波动被不同类型的投资者放大了。在我们模型最简单的版本里，有三类投资者。

turns.en: We start off with this valuation, value-based fundamental investor, which we know are out there, Warren Buffett having been one of them, but then we add two other types that are very prevalent in the marketplace.
turns.zh: 我们先有那个基于估值的、看重基本面的价值型投资者，我们知道这类人确实存在，Warren Buffett 就是其中之一；然后我们加上市场上极其普遍的两类。

turns.en: One of them, there can be no doubt of whatsoever, it's a static investor. We know that so many investors out there have a static strategic asset allocation.
turns.zh: 第一类是毫无疑问的，就是静态型投资者（static investor）。我们知道太多投资者有一套固定的战略资产配置。

turns.en: Maybe 60% equities, 40% fixed income or 70, 30 or endowments have these pretty strategic asset allocations. Over time, they're just rebalancing back to those more or less.
turns.zh: 也许 60% 股票、40% 债券，或者 70/30，大学捐赠基金也有各自相当固定的战略资产配置。长期看，他们只是不断再平衡回这些比例。

turns.en: They will move somewhat over time, but not much. We can think of them as static. Their behavior exacerbates any exogenous changes in supply and demand that take place, but then really the critical key investor type that we believe is generating so much of the perceived market anomalies is the extrapolative investor, the return chaser, the investor who comes up with their expected return for the market based on what the market has done
turns.zh: 他们会随时间有一些变化，但不多，可以视作静态。他们的行为会放大任何外生的供需变化。但真正关键的、我们认为制造了大量所谓市场异象的投资者类型，是外推型投资者（extrapolator），也就是追逐收益的人：他们对市场预期回报的判断，来自市场近期的表现。

turns.en: recently. We call them extrapolators and we say they make their asset allocation decisions based on recent returns, not just using recent returns exactly as they've been with some squeezing, with some rational use of that historical return, but when historical returns are higher, they want to own more equities and when historical returns are lower, they want to own less equities.
turns.zh: 我们把他们叫外推型投资者。他们根据近期回报来做资产配置决策——不是把近期历史回报原样拿来用，中间会有一些压缩、一些对历史回报的理性运用——但当历史回报高时，他们就想多持有股票；历史回报低时，就想少持有股票。

turns.en: Those guys combined with the static guys just overwhelm this fundamental investor and give us so many of the behavioral things that we see in the marketplace.
turns.zh: 这帮人加上静态那帮人，完全压倒了基本面投资者，产生了我们在市场上看到的大量行为现象。

turns.en: Can you go into a little bit more detail about why static investors are exacerbating the demand trucks? Just take a simple example that we can follow with words without a blackboard or anything.
turns.zh: 能再详细讲讲为什么静态型投资者会放大需求的冲击吗？我们就用一个用语言就能跟上的简单例子，不用黑板什么的。

turns.en: Imagine that the marketplace is only made up of static investors that want to be 50% in stocks and 50% in fixed income. That's where they are.
turns.zh: 想象市场上只有静态型投资者，他们想保持 50% 股票、50% 固收。他们就停在这个比例上。

turns.en: Then some companies turn up and they're like, we need to buy back our stock because that's what we want to do with our excess cash flow. We're going to buy back our stock.
turns.zh: 然后有些公司站出来说：我们要回购自家股票，因为我们想把多余现金流用来回购。

turns.en: They decide just let's keep the numbers as simple as possible even though they're a little bit unrealistic. Let's say that companies want to buy back 10% of all outstanding equities.
turns.zh: 我们就把数字弄得尽可能简单，哪怕有点不现实。假设公司想回购全部流通股票的 10%。

turns.en: We know that the only place they can buy them from is the static investors because that's our only investor class. They have $50, the static investors have $50 of stocks, they have to sell $5 of stocks to the companies buying back their stock that are buying back 10% of the whole marketplace.
turns.zh: 我们知道它们唯一能买到的地方就是静态型投资者手里，因为那是我们唯一的投资者类别。静态型投资者手里有 50 块钱的股票，他们必须卖 5 块钱的股票给这些回购 10% 市值的公司。

turns.en: Now they're left with what? They're left with, if market prices don't move, they have $45 of stock and $55 of cash or fixed income. What has to happen is that their $45 of stock has to become worth $55 because they want to be 50-50.
turns.zh: 那他们剩下什么？如果市场价格不动，他们手里就剩 45 块股票、55 块现金或固收。必须发生的是，他们那 45 块股票得变成值 55 块，因为他们想保持 50/50。

turns.en: The only way that can happen, they can't trade with each other, that doesn't help anything. The only way that that could happen is the price of the stock market has to go up not by 10% but by 20% because we have to go from 45 to 55, which is $10 on 45, call it 20%.
turns.zh: 这唯一的实现方式是股价得涨，不是涨 10%，而是涨 20%，因为要从 45 变到 55，是 45 块钱上多了 10 块，差不多 20%。

turns.en: If companies are buying back 1% of their stock, stock prices are going to have to go up 2% if the only investors are the static weight strategic investors and if they're a 50-50 weight.
turns.zh: 如果公司回购 1% 的股票，而市场上只有静态战略配置的投资者、又是 50/50 的配置，股价就得涨 2%。

turns.en: If their asset allocation were 60-40 or 40-60 or whatever, it would be a little bit different. That shows you how the numbers work and it's really simple like that.
turns.zh: 如果他们的配置是 60/40 或 40/60，数字会略有不同。这展示了数字是怎么算出来的，就是这么简单。

turns.en: We've heard a lot about that, the inelastic demand from investors over the last couple of years as we've explored the effective index funds on financial markets.
turns.zh: 过去几年我们一直在讨论投资者需求的无弹性，讨论被动指数基金对金融市场的影响。

turns.en: I guess they'd be a good example of that static investor. Yes. We talk about the Gabbai and Kojian paper in our article. They came at it a different way.
turns.zh: 被动指数基金应该算是这种静态投资者的一个很好的例子。对。我们文章里讨论了 Gabaix 和 Koijen 的那篇论文，他们的切入角度不一样。

turns.en: Many different practitioners and observers think about what this elasticity is. Our number is lower than the Gabbai-Kojian one, it's like half of that or so.
turns.zh: 很多从业者和观察者都在想这个弹性到底是多少。我们给出的数字比 Gabaix-Koijen 的小，大概只有他们的一半。

turns.en: We think that 1% might cause a 1% move in the market, exogenous change in demand. They're two or three times bigger. One of the most interesting things from their research was when they sent out a survey question to like 50 or 100 economists and they said, imagine that there's some investor that needs to buy 10 basis points worth of stocks.
turns.zh: 我们认为 1% 的外生需求变化可能让市场动 1%。他们的数字是我们的两三倍。他们研究里最有趣的一点是：他们给大概 50 到 100 位经济学家发了一个问卷，说假设有个投资者需要买入价值 10 个基点（bps）的股票。

turns.en: How much will that move stock prices? The vast majority of financial economists said zero, that the marketplace is perfectly elastic. I just thought that was so telling and interesting in terms of where we've been and how things are changing in terms of our understanding of stock market behavior.
turns.zh: 这会让股价涨多少？绝大多数金融经济学家回答：零，市场是完全有弹性的。我觉得这一点太有说明性、太有趣了——它反映了我们曾经在哪里，以及我们对股市行为的理解正在怎样变化。

turns.en: Yeah, that's really interesting. In the basic form of the model you mentioned that there are three investor types, the value investor, the static investor, and the performance-chasing investor, can you talk about the effect that each investor type has on the market?
turns.zh: 是啊，真有意思。你说模型的基本形式里有三类投资者：价值型、静态型、追绩型。能分别讲讲每类投资者对市场的影响吗？

turns.en: As we said already, the value investor is kind of stabilizing things a little bit, but the extrapolator is pushing the other way. The market goes up.
turns.zh: 就像我们已经说的，价值型投资者在稍微稳定局面，但外推型投资者在往反方向推。市场上涨，

turns.en: They want to own more equities and this is making it more difficult to reach an equilibrium. The extrapolators are creating momentum in the price series.
turns.zh: 他们就想多买股票，这让均衡更难达成。外推型投资者正在制造价格序列里的动量。

turns.en: They're also creating this excess volatility. When you have a fundamental positive shock like earnings are going to be higher, everybody wants to buy more stocks, the fundamental guys do, the static guys do because they want to get back to their whatever 50-50 weight and the extrapolators do because the market's gone up and so they have a higher expected return.
turns.zh: 他们也在制造这种超额波动。当出现一个基本面的正向冲击——比如盈利要变高——所有人都想买更多股票：价值型想买，静态型也想买，因为想回到 50/50；外推型想买，因为市场涨了、他们的预期回报更高了。

turns.en: They're the primary cause of these behaviors that we're seeing and it's really these exogenous shocks eventually can cause things to turn around, but it's a pretty fine balance.
turns.zh: 我们看到的这些行为，主因就是他们。说到底，还是这些外生冲击最终可能让局面逆转，但这之间的平衡相当微妙。

turns.en: When we look at US stock market performance, a number of observers have pointed out that this tremendous US stock market performance over the last three decades has primarily been driven by compression in valuation, I mean lower earnings yield a higher PE rather than the earnings growth.
turns.zh: 看美股的长期表现，不少观察者指出，过去 30 年美股惊人的回报，主要驱动力是估值压缩——盈利收益率（earnings yield）下降、市盈率上升——而不是盈利增长。

turns.en: I mean earnings growth of US stocks versus non-US stocks has been faster, but also you have to take away the effect of buybacks in making that earnings growth look faster than it really is, but earnings growth has been good, but really it's this compression and the risk premium that's given us a very large part of this tremendous performance we've had over the last 30 years in US stocks.
turns.zh: 我是说，美股相对非美股的盈利增长确实更快，但你也得剔除回购对盈利增长的粉饰。盈利增长是不错，但真正贡献过去 30 年美股巨大回报的，主要是这个估值压缩、是风险溢价。

turns.en: Of the three investor types, which one performs the best? None of them do great. The static investor just gets the return of the market over the long term and it's okay.
turns.zh: 那三类投资者里，哪一类表现最好？都不怎么样。静态型投资者长期就拿市场回报，还行。

turns.en: The extrapolator kind of does poorly because ultimately it all catches up with them. They're not following a super rational strategy, but the value investor does a little bit better than the static investor, but not hugely because they just have to suffer through these really long periods where the expected risk premium is low, but the market is going up, up, up.
turns.zh: 外推型做得不太好，因为迟早要还的，他们用的不是多么理性的策略。价值型比静态型好一点，但好得不多，因为他们得熬过那些风险溢价明明很低、市场却涨涨涨的漫长时间。

turns.en: None of those investor types do great, but there are some investment strategies that do better, which we can get to, but it's surprising in one way that the value investors don't do great, but we kind of know that also from history too.
turns.zh: 这三类都不算出色，但有些投资策略会更好，这个我们可以聊。但价值型不突出这一点还是让人意外——不过从历史上我们也多少知道这一点。

turns.en: We know that getting really underweight equities when the risk premium is low is a difficult position to take and doesn't create a much higher sharp ratio and much better returns.
turns.zh: 我们知道，在风险溢价很低的时候大幅低配股票，是个很难坚持的位置，它并不能带来高得多的夏普比率（Sharpe ratio）和好得多的回报。

turns.en: It's better in the long run, but it's not as much better as I might imagine. What's the impact of wealth moving between the investor types over time?
turns.zh: 长期看更好，但没有我想象中好那么多。那财富在不同投资者类型之间转移，会有什么影响？

turns.en: We've modeled these kind of exogenous shocks where each investor type is getting some extra cash or needs to spend some cash generating this noise trading, this idea that somebody needs to buy a house or somebody needs to pay for college or somebody got a big bonus and was investigating in the market.
turns.zh: 我们模拟过这类外生冲击：每类投资者拿到一些额外的钱、或者要花掉一些钱——这就是所谓噪声交易，比如有人要买房、有人要交学费、有人拿了大额奖金进市场。

turns.en: We've tried to model pretty heavy flows and not the same flows between the different types of investor to get some of that noise, but I think what you'd expect when the extrapolators are getting more capital either because of some exogenous cash flow shocks or because they're just doing so well because they're riding a good trend, then the market behavior that we see from them gets more exaggerated.
turns.zh: 我们尝试模拟比较大规模的资金流动，在不同类型投资者之间流动得不一样，来获取那种噪声。但我想你会预期：当外推型拿到更多资金——不管是外生现金流冲击，还是因为他们搭上一波好趋势赚得好——他们的行为造成的市场现象就更夸张。

turns.en: One of the challenges in building our model was that in early versions of it, things would just blow up. All of a sudden, the price would just go to infinity because the extrapolators got all the money and there was nobody that they could trade with, so there was no price, but as we made it more realistic, we found that the simulations that we were running behave much better as well, but it is a fine balance.
turns.zh: 建模型的一个挑战是：早期版本里，模型动不动就爆炸。价格突然冲到无穷大，因为钱全被外推型赚走了，没有对手方可以交易，于是就没有价格了。但随着我们把模型做得更真实，模拟的表现也好多了。不过这确实是一个微妙的平衡。

turns.en: Really interesting. Can you talk a little bit about momentum and extrapolation and how those two things are not the same? I love this topic.
turns.zh: 真有意思。能讲讲动量和外推为什么不是一回事吗？这个话题我特别喜欢。

turns.en: Twelve years ago, I was at a conference where Rob Arnott was speaking to an audience and he said, the number one thing that people do to shoot themselves in the foot is to be return chasers.
turns.zh: 12 年前，我在一个会议上听 Rob Arnott 演讲，他说，投资者自我伤害的头号行为，就是当追逐收益的人。

turns.en: This is the number one behavioral foyable of investors. Right around that time, I had been reading the research on time series momentum and I was thinking to myself, how amazing that at the same time as Rob is saying this, which I agree with, at the same time, other researchers were saying the most salient anomaly, the single best thing you could have done as an investor historically is to be a momentum
turns.zh: 这是投资者第一号行为错误（behavioral foible）。差不多那段时间，我一直在读时序动量（time series momentum）的研究，我就想：太神奇了，Rob 说的这点我完全同意，而同一时间，另一批研究者却说，最显着的异象、历史上投资者能做的最好的一件事，就是当动量

turns.en: investor. That momentum has been everywhere and at all times. Time series momentum in particular is what I'm talking about here as opposed to cross-sectional.
turns.zh: 投资者。动量无处不在、无时不在。我这里说的是时序动量，而不是截面动量（cross-sectional momentum）。

turns.en: Right around that time, there were all these papers coming out or a number of papers looking at long-term time series momentum and how prevalent it was everywhere and everything.
turns.zh: 就在那段时间，涌现了很多论文，或者说好几篇论文，研究长期时序动量在多大程度上无处不在。

turns.en: Every commodity, every equity, et cetera, and I was like, why do these things sound exactly the same? How could it be that one of them is the worst thing and the other one is the best thing?
turns.zh: 每种商品、每只股票等等。我就纳闷：这两件事听起来怎么一模一样？怎么一个是坏事之最，另一个是好事之最？

turns.en: What I realized is that, first of all, momentum has a fully agreed upon definition. When we talk about momentum, more or less, we're all talking about the same thing.
turns.zh: 我意识到，首先，动量有一个完全公认的、统一的定义。我们谈动量时，大家说的基本是同一个东西。

turns.en: If you measure momentum slightly differently as a one-year moving average or as a one-year lookback or as a six-month lookback or whatever, you get the same results.
turns.zh: 你用略微不同的方式衡量动量——比如一年移动平均、一年回看期、六个月回看期——结果都差不多。

turns.en: But return chasing is a little bit more like when we see it, we know there is not a definition of return chasing. What is this return chasing behavior?
turns.zh: 但追逐收益就有点像：我们看到它，但没有任何关于追逐收益的定义。这种追逐收益的行为到底是什么？

turns.en: A number of observers have put forward ideas about why return chasing hurts and momentum helps. Cliff Asnes has one of the more remarked, repeated ideas of what return chasing is.
turns.zh: 不少观察者提出了追逐收益为什么有害而动量为什么有帮助的看法。Cliff Asness 提出了一个被引用和重复最多的想法，来说明追逐收益是什么。

turns.en: He says return chasing is momentum investing, but with a five-year lookback. I don't know how that stacks up in cross-sectional momentum, and maybe that's where Cliff is referring to it as being an explanation, so I can't speak there.
turns.zh: 他说，追逐收益就是拿五年回看期的动量投资。我不知道这在截面动量里成不成立，也许 Cliff 指的是那个语境下的解释，这个我说不好。

turns.en: But in time series momentum, that's not really a good explanation. We don't really see somebody following a five-year lookback with a binary momentum strategy as really being the worst thing that they could do.
turns.zh: 但在时序动量里，那不是个好解释。我们其实并不会看到一个人跟着五年回看期做二元动量策略，然后被折腾得最惨。

turns.en: It's not a good thing. It's not helping them, but it's not crushing them. So there's something else I think that's at work here. The way that we define return chasing or what we see as return chasing is the way we've modeled it in the paper and the way we've talked about it in previous papers, because we've been writing about this for maybe almost eight or 10 years, is that it's this more gradual thing, that momentum is a binary.
turns.zh: 那不是好事。它没有帮他，但也没有把他压垮。所以我觉得还有别的机制在起作用。我们对追逐收益的定义——或者说我们看到的追逐收益——就是我们在论文里建模的方式，之前几篇论文也讲过。我们写这个主题写了大概八到十年了——它是那种更渐进的东西，而动量是二元的。

turns.en: It's either your overweight or your underweight's binary. As soon as momentum flips one way or the other, you do that. With return chasing, it's this more gradual thing.
turns.zh: 动量要么是重仓要么是轻仓，是二元的。动量信号一翻转，你就切换。而追逐收益是那种更渐进的东西。

turns.en: When we model it in this research that we've done, you're looking at historical returns, and the better historical returns are, the more you want to own of equities.
turns.zh: 在我们的研究建模里，你看的是历史回报：历史回报越好，你就越想买更多股票。

turns.en: As the market's going up, historical returns are getting better, you're getting more and more and more overweight equities. Then now the market starts to go down and returns start to look not as good and worse and worse and worse, and now you're unloading.
turns.zh: 市场上涨时，历史回报越来越好，你越来越大幅超配股票。然后市场开始下跌，回报看起来越来越差，你开始减仓。

turns.en: Is that behavior which is different from the momentum trading that basically results in the return chasers doing poorly and the momentum guys doing well?
turns.zh: 这种行为和动量交易不同，正是它导致追绩的人表现差、做动量的人表现好吗？

turns.en: I have to caveat this really importantly, that it really depends on the relative size of these guys, because if the return chasers are just a few guys doing that and everybody else has their money in these momentum strategies, well then we don't get that anymore because everybody's having impact in this framework and in the real world we think there's a lot of impact from people trading large size.
turns.zh: 这里我必须加一个非常重要的前提：这真的取决于这几帮人的相对规模。如果追逐收益的只是几个人，其他所有人的钱都在动量策略里，那就不是那样了，因为在这个框架里，所有人的交易都有冲击；而在现实世界，我们认为大资金的交易冲击很大。

turns.en: It's this behavior that I've described and also it's the fact or what we think is the fact that the return chasing behavior is operating on a lot more capital than the momentum strategy than time series momentum is in general.
turns.zh: 就是我描述的这种行为，再加上我们认为的一个事实：追逐收益这种行为所操控的资金量，远大于时序动量策略。

turns.en: The beautiful thing about time series momentum in terms of why I think it generally doesn't get too big is because it just seems ridiculous.
turns.zh: 时序动量有个美妙的特性，这也是为什么我认为它通常不会做得太大——因为它看起来实在太荒谬了。

turns.en: I thought the thing was we're supposed to buy low and sell high and this strategy is sell low and buy high, that when time series momentum is working people are like, oh this is great I love it, but as soon as it stops working, as soon as you go through one or two years where time series momentum doesn't work, people are saying, I knew this was the stupidest thing ever, of course it would never work and they pull their money out.
turns.zh: 我原以为我们该低买高卖，而这个策略是低卖高买。当时序动量赚钱的时候，人们说：哇，太好了我爱它。可一旦它不灵了——只要经历一两年时序动量失效——人们就说：我早知道这是史上最蠢的东西，它当然不可能管用。然后把钱撤走。

turns.en: Now I think people's attitudes are changing over that, probably there's been so much research and talk, I think people are sticking with it maybe longer than before, but I think it just has a bit of trouble in attracting large amounts of capital for the long term because it's just something that people like as long as it works and when it doesn't work they flee and that has that impact.
turns.zh: 现在我觉得大家对它的态度在变。可能是因为研究和讨论太多了，人们也许比以前更能坚持。但我认为它还是很难长期吸引大量资金，因为人们对它的态度是：管用就喜欢，不管用就跑。这就带来了那种冲击。

turns.en: I don't know, at some point this time series momentum could just be the dominant force and then everything would be different. The performance chasers, the extrapolators, are they creating the momentum factor?
turns.zh: 谁知道呢，说不定哪天时序动量成了主导力量，那一切就都不一样了。那追逐业绩的外推型投资者，是不是动量因子的创造者？

turns.en: Yes, they'd be creating. It's their impact that's creating that evolution of prices that allows the momentum guys to make money. They're cumulatively buying more and more of the asset class pushing its price up and up and the momentum folks are seeing that signal with their more defined look back period and they're buying the thing that's going up.
turns.zh: 是的，他们就是创造者。正是他们的冲击塑造了价格的演变，让做动量的人能赚到钱。他们在累积地越买越多这类资产，把价格越推越高；而动量选手用他们更明确的回看期捕捉到信号，去买那个在涨的东西。

turns.en: They're getting ahead of it. You could think of them as front running that trend on average, relies on the momentum guys not having too much impact.
turns.zh: 他们抢在前面。你可以认为他们平均在抢先一步搭上趋势，前提是动量选手自己的冲击不太大。

turns.en: That works until it doesn't, which sucks. People get whipsawed and they lose a bunch of money in momentum and then they bail on momentum and the fact that that happens, it's almost like a bit of a risk premium story, not different, but people get blown out of momentum and that's why that it has continued to work.
turns.zh: 这能一直管用直到不管用——那很糟。人们被来回打脸，在动量上亏一大笔，然后弃动量而去。这件事会发生，几乎像一个风险溢价的故事——没有本质不同——人们被洗出动量策略，这也正是动量能持续有效的原因。

turns.en: Is that the right mechanism? I think that's one explanation. There's another explanation too, which is worth discussing, which is that when we talk about risk assets, when we talk about equities and things that are like equities, risk assets, the other thing that we know is that volatility tends to be skewed, that we have high vol when the market goes down and low vol when the market is going up and when it's grinding
turns.zh: 这个机制对吗？我觉得这是一种解释。还有另一个解释也值得一提：我们谈风险资产，谈股票和类似股票的东西——风险资产时，我们还知道的一件事是，波动率是偏斜的：市场跌的时候波动高，市场涨、尤其是磨磨蹭蹭上涨的时候波动低。当它磨磨

turns.en: higher. Momentum also happens to be correlated with the strategy of vol targeting. If you're doing vol targeting where you reduce exposure when the market becomes more volatile and you increase exposure when the market is calmer, then you're also following a bit of a momentum strategy, not a bit.
turns.zh: 蹭蹭走高时，波动就低。而动量恰好和波动率目标策略（vol targeting）高度相关。如果你做波动率目标管理——市场波动变大时降低敞口，市场更平静时提高敞口——那你也在跟随一种动量策略。不只是有一点。

turns.en: You're highly correlated with somebody who's following a momentum strategy. That vol targeting, in our opinion, is a very rational, logical thing to do.
turns.zh: 你和跟随动量策略的人高度相关。而波动率目标管理，在我们看来，是一个非常理性、非常合乎逻辑的做法。

turns.en: It goes back to the Merton share, it goes back to normal scaling logic of the higher, my sharp ratio, the more exposure I want, which means the higher the expected risk premium I want more and the higher the risk I want less.
turns.zh: 它回到 Merton share，回到那个归一化逻辑：我的夏普比率越高，我想要的风险敞口就越多——也就是预期风险溢价越高越想加，风险越高越想减。

turns.en: Vol targeting, to the extent that momentum is rhyming with vol targeting, it makes sense that it also is working and that it's helping to generate better risk adjusted returns for investors if you're following momentum with risk assets like equities, like oil, like REITs.
turns.zh: 所以只要动量和波动率目标管理是同韵的，它也能赚钱就说得通了，而且它有助于为投资者创造更好的风险调整后回报——只要你是在股票、原油、REITs 这类风险资产上做动量。

turns.en: There's that also, which I think is really, really important as well. We wrote an article a while ago where some investment bank was saying, what you really should do is when VIX goes above 30%, when volatility is above 30, you should really load up on equities, which is the opposite of vol targeting.
turns.zh: 还有这一点，我认为同样非常非常重要。我们之前写过一篇文章，有家投行说：VIX 超过 30%、波动率高于 30 的时候，你其实该重仓股票——这恰恰是波动率目标管理的反面。

turns.en: We showed just through the simple back test of how the strategy would have done that doesn't generate a higher sharp ratio. We also talked about that logic as well.
turns.zh: 我们只是用一个简单的回测就展示了，那个策略并不能产生更高的夏普比率。我们也讨论了背后的逻辑。

turns.en: Maybe for somebody who's thinking, oh, when the market goes down and vol goes up, I want to buy. Well, when the market goes down and vol goes up, you want to sell.
turns.zh: 对有这种想法的人——哦，市场跌、波动升的时候我就该买——我要说：市场跌、波动升的时候，你其实该卖。

turns.en: When the market goes down and expected returns are higher, you want to buy. You have these two competing factors and it depends on how much of one versus the other has happened.
turns.zh: 而当市场跌、预期回报更高时，你才该买。这里有两股相互较劲的力量，最终取决于哪一边变化得更多。

turns.en: It's better to separate those things than to simply say, when vol goes up, I want to buy. It's more like vol goes up, you should reduce and expected returns go up, you should want to increase.
turns.zh: 最好把这两件事分开，而不是简单说：波动一升我就买。更合理的说法是：波动升，你应该减仓；预期回报升，你才想加仓。

turns.en: Maybe just for the benefit of listeners who didn't listen to your last episode or have not heard us talk about the Merton share. Can you talk about the Merton share logic behind the statement that you just said?
turns.zh: 也许为了照顾没听过你上期节目、也没听我们聊过 Merton share 的听众，能讲讲你刚才那句话背后的 Merton share 逻辑吗？

turns.en: Merton and Paul Samuelson attacked the lifetime consumption and portfolio choice problem in the late 60s. They came up with this solution where under a very stringent and unrealistic set of assumptions in terms of how risk assets behave and all that, but it gives us a good rule of thumb, the amount of exposure you should want to have to risky assets in your portfolio is proportional to the expected risk premium that those risky assets are giving you.
turns.zh: Merton 和 Paul Samuelson 在 60 年代末攻克了生命周期消费与组合选择（lifetime consumption and portfolio choice）问题。他们给出了一个解，建立在非常苛刻、不现实的假设上——关于风险资产如何表现等等——但它给了我们一个很好的经验法则：你应该让风险资产在组合里的敞口，与这些风险资产给你的预期风险溢价成比例。

turns.en: You have to have an expected return and know what the safe asset is offering divided by the risk of those risky assets where you're measuring risk as variance.
turns.zh: 你得有一个预期回报，知道安全资产给多少收益，然后除以风险资产的波动，其中你用方差（variance）来衡量风险。

turns.en: Also you would scale that based upon your own personal degree of risk aversion. So there's a constant in there that's like your personal constant that you would divide by your degree of risk aversion.
turns.zh: 然后还要按你个人的风险厌恶程度来缩放。公式里有个常数，是你个人的常数，用它除以你的风险厌恶系数。

turns.en: That Merton share as we call it that also is actually the same as is a more inclusive version of the Kelly criterion where the Kelly criterion is the Merton share where that coefficient of risk aversion is equal to one and that gives you the Kelly criterion which comes at the problem from a different place but winds up in the same place.
turns.zh: 我们称之为 Merton share。它其实也就是 Kelly 标准（Kelly criterion）一个更一般化的版本：Kelly criterion 就是风险厌恶系数等于 1 时的 Merton share。Kelly criterion 从另一个角度切入问题，但殊途同归。

turns.en: Another way to think about the Merton share that might be easier is that the amount of risk that you want is proportional to the sharp ratio of the risky asset portfolio that you want to invest in and then that's the amount of risk you want and then to figure out how much exposure you want, how much of those assets you want, then you would divide by their risk and that's why we wind up with risk squared with standard deviation of return
turns.zh: 理解 Merton share 还有一个可能更容易的方式：你想要的风险量，与你想投的风险资产组合的夏普比率成比例。这就是你想要的风险量。然后再算你想要多少敞口、持有多少这种资产，就除以它们的风险。这就是为什么分母会出现风险的平方、也就是回报标准差

turns.en: squared and the denominator. Again, it's a rule of thumb but it ties expected utility theory to the investment process. We can get more general and more realistic but that's the simple rule of thumb from Bob Merton and well Paul Samuelson's paper too but I think Bob, we call it the Merton share because I think Bob kind of came up with it and then Professor Samuelson was his mentor.
turns.zh: 的平方。再次强调，这只是经验法则，但它把期望效用理论和投资流程接上了。我们可以做得更一般、更贴近现实，但这是 Bob Merton——也包括 Paul Samuelson 那篇论文——给的简单经验法则。我想 Bob 是这样来的：我们叫它 Merton share，是因为我觉得主要是 Bob 想出来的，而 Samuelson 教授是他的导师。

turns.en: They published joint papers at the same time but I think that Bob came up with it in continuous time first is what I understand but I'm not sure.
turns.zh: 他们同时发表了合著的论文，但据我理解，Bob 是先在连续时间框架下提出这个的，不过我不确定。

turns.en: Yeah, I don't know. I've seen it called the Merton Samuelson share too. I don't know how much it matters. I've never heard Bob complain about it being called one of the...
turns.zh: 是，我也不清楚。我见过它被叫作 Merton-Samuelson share。我觉得叫什么都无所谓。反正我没听 Bob 抱怨过别人叫它……

turns.en: Yeah, either way. Yup. A really good explanation and it's really interesting how that ties into momentum and the persistence of momentum because people are changing their asset allocations as risk and expects of return evolve and that is driving momentum and momentum should then persist unless it becomes the dominant where most of the capital sits, I guess.
turns.zh: 对，叫什么不重要。这个解释非常好。有意思的是，它和动量、和动量的持续性是怎么连上的：因为人们会随着风险和预期回报的变化调整资产配置，这本身就在驱动动量；所以动量应该会继续存在——除非它变成大多数资金所在的那个主导策略。

turns.en: Yes. Super interesting. When we were talking about other investors that could do better, one simple strategy that actually does really well is a value and momentum combination.
turns.zh: 没错，太有意思了。刚才说到有其他投资者能做得更好，有一个非常简单的策略其实表现非常好：价值和动量的组合。

turns.en: So combining fundamental long-term cash flow investing signals with momentum. So value and momentum gets a much higher sharp ratio when you combine those two and this really goes to explain in some ways very satisfyingly the results from the as in this et al paper, I forget when it's from, but value and momentum everywhere that I think has had an impact everywhere on people's thinking.
turns.zh: 把基本面长期现金流的信号和动量结合起来。价值和动量一组合，夏普比率就高得多。这也在某种程度上非常圆满地解释了 Asness 等人那篇论文的结果——我忘了是哪一年的——但价值和动量无处不在（value and momentum everywhere）那篇文章，影响了几乎所有想法的人。

turns.en: I mean, I think that was a really seminal papers certainly shaped our thoughts a lot at Elm. What do you think your model adds to our understanding of markets?
turns.zh: 我是说，我认为那是一篇开创性的论文，肯定对我们在 Elm 的思考影响很大。你觉得你们的模型为我们理解市场增加了什么？

turns.en: There's a vast, vast literature of these heterogeneous agent model approaches to the markets and from the Santa Fe Institute to Northeastern universities and there's all kinds of contributions here.
turns.zh: 关于这类异质代理人模型（heterogeneous agent model）的市场研究，有海量的文献，从圣塔菲研究所（Santa Fe Institute）到 Northeastern 这样的大学，各种各样的贡献都有。

turns.en: And I think that the two things that we really add to our understanding about this is that number one is that we're presenting this in a way that's much easier for people to understand that there's not heavy math here.
turns.zh: 我觉得我们为理解这件事增加的主要是两点：第一，我们用更容易理解的方式呈现它，没有高深的数学。

turns.en: All of the most recent papers use a lot of heavy math and they're really hard for most people to comprehend. And then the early papers were more like stick models, Larry Summers and DeLong Summers et cetera, Schleifer kind of had a stick model early on because they were just kind of showing the general contours of what things look like in a multi-agent setting.
turns.zh: 最近的那些论文都用很重的数学，大多数人根本看不懂。而早期的论文更像稻草人模型，Larry Summers、DeLong 和 Summers 那些人，还有 Shleifer，早期就是稻草人式的模型，只是勾勒一下多代理人环境下的大致轮廓。

turns.en: So one is that we've made it more accessible and then the other one is that we've made it more general. Nobody as far as we know has built a model that has six or seven different kinds of investors in there.
turns.zh: 所以，第一是我们让它更容易接近。第二是我们让它更一般化。据我们所知，没人建过一个包含六七种不同类型投资者的模型。

turns.en: We have the three that we talked about. We have a value and momentum investor. We have a by the dip short-term reversal investor. We've modeled like a more anticipatory investor in there as well.
turns.zh: 我们有刚说的三种。我们有价值+动量型投资者。我们有逢低买入（buy the dip）的短期反转（short-term reversal）型投资者。我们还建模了一种更前瞻性的投资者。

turns.en: So this kind of generality of the broadness of it going and allowing you to put in any kind of investor as you want and was going to help people who want to take the research further and put in more realistic investor types and make the simulation more and more realistic.
turns.zh: 所以这种广度、这种一般性，让你可以往里加任何你想加的投资者类型。这会给想把研究往前推进的人提供帮助——加入更真实的投资者类型，让模拟越来越贴近现实。

turns.en: You mentioned the value and momentum insight. How else do you think through in writing down this model effect your views on asset allocation?
turns.zh: 你提到了价值+动量这个洞见。除此之外，写下这个模型还怎样影响了你对资产配置的思考？

turns.en: That's perhaps the main one, but I think when you come to appreciate how important extrapolators are to what's happening in the world, maybe it's a little bit of to a man with a hammer every problem is a nail, but it just feels like understanding these extrapolators and how much they can affect behavior creates a lot more humility in terms of what the markets can and might do and also gives you this focus in terms of trying to understand what's putting
turns.zh: 那也许是最大的一点。但我觉得，当你体会到外推型对正在发生的事情有多重要时——可能有点拿着锤子的人看什么都是钉子——但理解这些外推型以及他们能多么深刻地影响行为，会让你对市场能做什么、可能会做什么，多一份谦卑。而且它给你一个焦点，去理解到底是什么在

turns.en: more focus on them than on any other investor type and behavior in terms of trying to understand what's going on. So, so many people, long-term market observers, they look and they say, gosh, I don't understand what's going on.
turns.zh: 给他们、而不是给任何其他投资者类型和行为，施加更大的权重。很多长期观察市场的人看着行情说：天哪，我看不懂现在在发生什么。

turns.en: We have higher interest rates. We have this bad government deficit. We have tariffs. We have global political instability. All these different things we have going on and they're like, I don't understand why the market is 20% higher after all these things have happened.
turns.zh: 利率更高了，政府赤字这么糟，有关税，全球政治不稳定，发生了这么多事，他们就想：为什么在这些事情发生之后，市场还高了 20%？

turns.en: What is going on? To us thinking with this lens on, it's like, well, one simple explanation is that until recently US companies were buying back over a trillion dollars of their stock per year.
turns.zh: 到底怎么回事？对我们来说，戴上这个透镜去想，一个很简单的解释是：直到不久前，美国公司每年还在回购超过一万亿美元的自家股票。

turns.en: There were no IPOs flows into 401ks and so on. We're also running at like a trillion dollars. So here was a couple of percent of the total or more than a couple of percent of the total US market disappearing or being bought by exogenous demand each year.
turns.zh: 几乎没有 IPO，钱不断流进 401(k)，如此种种。这也差不多是每年一万亿美元的量级。所以每年有多达几个百分点、甚至更多的美股市值，被这种外生需求买走或者吸走。

turns.en: Combine that with people just seeing these returns and I mean, I don't know how many people I've heard just say, just keep all your money in equities because you're going to get 10% a year.
turns.zh: 再加上人们只是看着这些回报——我都不知道听过多少人直接说：把钱全放股票里就行了，你一年能赚 10%。

turns.en: It's been 10% a year for 100 years and it's going to be 10% a year forever. That's self-reinforcing for a long time. For some indeterminate amount of time.
turns.zh: 一百年都是年化 10%，以后也会永远年化 10%。这种自我强化会持续很长时间，持续多久则说不清。

turns.en: Another thing that we kind of tried to play around with in the model is there is some time when there's probably some time when you can get a lot of supply of equities.
turns.zh: 我们在模型里还试着琢磨过另一件事：可能有些时候，股票的供给会大量出现。

turns.en: When it looks like the long term expected return of equities is below government bonds, we would anticipate that companies will issue a lot of equity.
turns.zh: 当股票的长期预期回报看起来低于政府债券时，我们会预期公司大量发行股票。

turns.en: When it really becomes clear, when equity becomes cheaper than debt, company treasurers, company CFOs, company CEOs and boards pay attention and they're like, okay, we should raise equity.
turns.zh: 什么时候会变得很清楚？当股票比债务便宜的时候。公司财务主管、CFO、CEO 和董事会是会注意到的，他们会说：好，我们该发股票了。

turns.en: There's a lot we can do when equity costs less than debt and we still, the market would need to go up quite a bit more to get there, but there is some boundary condition I think that's out there.
turns.zh: 股票比债务便宜的时候，我们能做很多事。当然，市场还得再涨不少才会到那一步。但我认为外面存在某种边界条件。

turns.en: Japan hit that boundary condition in the late 80s. Boy, did they issue a lot of equity in the late 80s in Japan, right? They issued a lot of equity in that run up.
turns.zh: 日本在 80 年代末就撞上了那个边界条件。天哪，日本 80 年代末可真是发了大量股票，对吧？在那轮上涨里发了很多股票。

turns.en: We've got a ways to go still is what you're saying. We have a ways, maybe it's another 50% up all else equal or a percent or two higher in interest rates.
turns.zh: 你的意思是，我们离那儿还远。是，还有一段路，也许再涨 50%，在其他条件不变的情况下；或者利率再高一个或两个百分点。

turns.en: If we got 10-year tips at three and a half, 10-year treasuries at six, we'd see more equity issuance. If the market stayed here, that is, they didn't go down.
turns.zh: 如果 10 年期 TIPS 到 3.5%、10 年期国债到 6%，而市场维持在这里——就是股票不再往下跌——我们会看到更多股票发行。

turns.en: Very interesting to think about. I haven't thought about US stock market valuations in a while because whenever we talk about it, the market just keeps going up.
turns.zh: 这很有意思，值得琢磨。我已经很久没认真思考美股估值了，因为每次我们聊这个话题，市场就继续涨。

turns.en: It's like, all right, maybe we're contributing to the extrapolation by no longer talking about it. Exactly. You did a great article on long short direct indexing.
turns.zh: 就是说：好吧，也许不聊估值，我们本身就在给外推添砖加瓦。没错。你们写过一篇很棒的文章，讲多空型直接指数化（long short direct indexing）。

turns.en: Can you talk a little bit for listeners just about what that is before we start asking you questions about it? There's been so much over the last couple of years in the US on different kinds of strategies to help people defer their taxes or in some cases, pay less taxes.
turns.zh: 在我们问问题之前，能不能先跟听众讲讲这是什么？过去几年美国有特别多这类帮人递延纳税、或者少缴税的各种策略。

turns.en: What we've had for quite a long time are direct indexed tax laws harvesting programs where you give your money to a company like Parametric, which I guess is now owned by somebody else and a lot of companies are offering it, and they put you into a portfolio of individual stocks like the S&P 500, and then when individual stocks go down, they sell them and then they try to buy them back later on to realize losses as much as they can and to try to track the
turns.zh: 我们已经有相当长时间见到直接指数化的税损收割（tax loss harvesting）项目：你把钱交给像 Parametric 这样的公司——我记得它现在被别人收购了——很多公司都在提供这个服务。他们给你一个类似标普 500 的一篮子个股组合，当某只个股下跌时，就卖掉它，之后再试图买回来，尽可能多地实现亏损，同时尽量跟踪

turns.en: S&P 500 over time while realizing loss as well. More recently, it's this strategy that people have thought about in the past is taking that to another level of let's go leveraged long stocks and run a short position against them.
turns.zh: 标普 500 的长期表现，顺便实现税收亏损。更近一些的是这种策略——过去也有人想过——就是把它再上一个台阶：用杠杆做多股票，同时开一个空头仓位对冲。

turns.en: Instead of just taking $100 and buying $100 of stocks, I could take $100 and control $300 or $400 of stocks, and I can get a lot more tax losses in that way to offset gains that I might have elsewhere.
turns.zh: 与其拿 100 块钱买 100 块钱股票，我可以拿 100 块钱控制 300 或 400 块钱的股票，这样能拿到多得多的税务亏损，去抵消我在别处的收益。

turns.en: This is called leveraged long short tax loss harvesting because it's using leverage and it's using shorting, but it's still tax loss harvesting with individual stocks.
turns.zh: 这叫杠杆多空税损收割（leveraged long short tax loss harvesting），因为它用了杠杆、又用了做空，但本质上还是用个股做税损收割。

turns.en: It's grown quite a bit. There's been a bunch of articles about it. We've been writing about this for a while. We started off writing about direct index tax loss harvesting, and we made the argument that most investors shouldn't really have a lot of capital gains.
turns.zh: 这个业务发展得挺快，也有很多文章写它。我们写这个话题也写了一阵子了。一开始我们写的是直接指数化税损收割，我们提出过一个论点：大多数投资者其实不该有太多资本利得。

turns.en: If they're long-term equity investors, they shouldn't have a lot of capital gains to worry about other than the fact that they are selling some stocks over time to consume.
turns.zh: 如果你是长期股票投资者，你本来就没有多少资本利得要操心——除了你为了消费，时间一长总要卖掉一些股票。

turns.en: The point of the wealth is to spend it, so you have to sell over time stuff that you have in a taxable account and realize some gains, but overall, if you are invested in stocks, you don't have a lot of capital gains, you're getting a lot of deferral just naturally.
turns.zh: 财富的意义就在于花掉它，所以你在应税账户里的东西，随时间总要卖一些、实现一些收益。但总的来说，如果你就持有股票，你并没有多少资本利得——递延本身就已经给你带来很多好处了。

turns.en: But if for any reason you do other kinds of investing, maybe in hedge funds or other things and you get realizations, you have a lot of capital gains, you might want to try to reduce your payment of them over time and defer those gains into the future.
turns.zh: 但如果你出于某种原因在做别的投资，比如对冲基金之类，会产生实际的利得实现、资本利得很多，那你就可能想减少为此缴税，把这些利得往后递延。

turns.en: We've written about this, and with respect to direct index tax loss harvesting, we've said, well, after you figure out the fees because this carries fees, and after you figure out the extra risk that you're bearing, you might be just as well off owning ETFs and doing tax loss harvesting on your ETFs, own Vanguard Broad, Total Market, and if that goes down, replace it with the S&P 500 index fund and do something like that, or maybe own the
turns.zh: 我们写过这个。关于直接指数化税损收割，我们说过：你先算清楚费用——这是要收费的——再算清楚你多承担的风险，其实你可能干脆持有 ETF、在 ETF 上做税损收割就好：持有 Vanguard 的全市场指数，它跌了就换成标普 500 指数基金，诸如此类；或者持有

turns.en: different sectors of the S&P 500 and do something like that. That takes you to about the same place. You have less risk, probably it's slightly better, but you just have less complexity.
turns.zh: 标普 500 不同行业的 ETF 做替换。你能达到的效果差不多。风险更低，可能还略好一点，而且简单得多。

turns.en: You don't wake up one day with a 400 stock portfolio that you don't know what to do with, where you have corporate actions and all this stuff, that you have flexibility by having a simple portfolio and you're getting about the same result.
turns.zh: 你不用某天早上醒来发现手里有个 400 只股票的组合，完全不知道拿它怎么办，还得处理公司行为等等那些破事。保持一个简单组合让你更灵活，结果也差不多。

turns.en: When there started to be more interest from people in leverage, long, short, direct indexing, we analyzed that and we came to a similar conclusion.
turns.zh: 当人们对杠杆多空直接指数化开始更有兴趣时，我们分析了它，得出的结论类似。

turns.en: The conclusion that we came to in our research was that if you don't believe that the long shorts are going to generate alpha, we don't really think it's worth doing.
turns.zh: 我们研究得出的结论是：如果你不相信这些多空头寸能产生 alpha，那它就不太值得做。

turns.en: The fees are much higher than in the unleveraged version because here you have higher fees from the manager and you also have a long, short friction that Fidelity or Schwab or whoever the custodian is charging to run the longs and shorts.
turns.zh: 费用比不加杠杆的版本高得多，因为这里管理费更高，而且还有 Fidelity、Schwab 或任何托管商针对多空操作收的摩擦费用。

turns.en: If you don't believe that there's alpha in this long short strategy, then probably it's not worth doing. I mean, we're not saying it's terrible, but it's just probably not worth doing and again, you get all this complexity and you're locked into this portfolio and it's messy for however long you're doing it.
turns.zh: 如果你认为这个多空策略里没有 alpha，那大概不值得做。我们不是说它糟透了，只是大概不值得。而且你又换来一大堆复杂性，被锁在这个组合里，在持有的这段时间里又乱又麻烦。

turns.en: That was our conclusion. We think there are special cases where this stuff can make sense for people. For instance, if you have a lot of short-term capital gains that some of these strategies could make sense to try to reduce those and create long-term capital gains out of them and get a conversion for US investors or if you're living in California and you're going to move to Alaska and you know that you're going to do that and it's like, I just want
turns.zh: 那就是我们的结论。我们认为有些特殊情况下，这种东西可以有意义。比如，你有很多短期资本利得，这类策略也许有助于把它们转化成美国投资者的长期资本利得；或者你住在加州，马上要搬到阿拉斯加，你确定你会搬，你就想

turns.en: to defer my gains for a few years because I'm going to a low tax state. Maybe that could make sense too, but in general, for most people and for young people in particular, we don't think it's really worth the squeeze.
turns.zh: 把利得递延几年，因为你要去一个低税州——这也可能有意义。但总体上，对大多数人、尤其对年轻人来说，我们不觉得值得费那个劲。

turns.en: It's interesting because we've written about this stuff and journalists have talked to us about it. The last time a journalist was talking to us about it, she was saying, well, can I quote you in this article?
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我们写过这些东西，也有记者来聊过。上次一个记者跟我们聊时说：这篇文章里我能引用你吗？

turns.en: And I was like, that people that get quoted in your articles really get some nasty stuff said about them in the public domain. So please, if you wouldn't mind, please don't mention my name.
turns.zh: 我说，能在你文章里被引用的人，之后在公共舆论里可没少被骂。所以如果你不介意的话，请不要提我的名字。

turns.en: I've had enough bad things said about me over my life. She said, well, but you have this research and I was like, yeah, I know, but still like if you don't mind.
turns.zh: 我这辈子被说的坏话已经够多了。她说，可你们有这项研究啊。我说，我知道，但还是希望你别写我。

turns.en: So then she said, well, who else could I talk to that's done this research and feels the same way that you do? And I was like, oh my goodness, there's nobody really that I can think of.
turns.zh: 然后她说，那还有谁做过这个研究、还有谁跟你持相同观点？我一琢磨：天哪，我真想不出还有谁。

turns.en: There should be somebody. And then I started to think, well, maybe we're just all wrong about this stuff. I don't know. But that's what we think.
turns.zh: 按理说应该有人做过才对。然后我开始想：也许是我们全搞错了？我不知道。但这就是我们的看法。

turns.en: We're not crazy about all this stuff. There's no holier than thou stuff going on here. We're just saying that if you don't think there's alpha there, then you don't really want to do it.
turns.zh: 我们对这些东西并没有深恶痛绝，也没有摆什么高人一等的姿态。我们只是说：如果你不觉得那里有 alpha，你就不该去做。

turns.en: I think there's alpha. Great. But then you kind of have to ask yourself a little bit the question of if you thought there was alpha there, why weren't you doing it to begin with?
turns.zh: 我觉得那里有 alpha。很好。但那你多少得问自己一个问题：如果你觉得有 alpha，你当初为什么自己不做？

turns.en: And you might say, well, I thought there was a little bit of alpha, but not enough to overcome the fees. And okay, you know, that's fine. But I think there has to be this question of, do you think that somebody can run long shorts in a systematic way and generate alpha?
turns.zh: 你可能会说：我觉得有一点 alpha，但不足以覆盖费用。好吧，那也行。但我觉得必须回答的问题是：你到底认为有人能系统地运行多空头寸并产生 alpha 吗？

turns.en: Maybe it's tough. We know that rent tech does it. We know that there's a bunch of people out there who do it. And generally, whoever you can be sure of that does it doesn't take outside investors.
turns.zh: 这也许很难。我们知道 RenTech 做得到，我们知道外面确实有一批人做得到。而且通常，那些你可以确信做得到的人，是不收外部投资人钱的。

turns.en: So we know that it's possible. But in general, it seems as though when somebody really cracks that nut, they very quickly send everybody's money back.
turns.zh: 所以我们知道这是可能的。但一般来说，似乎当有人真正破解这道题，他们很快就会把钱退还给投资人。

turns.en: So if somebody's still taking money to do it, maybe they found a way to do it in scale. It's possible. But everybody's entitled to their opinion about the alpha.
turns.zh: 所以如果有人还在对外募资做这件事，也许他们找到了规模化做到的方法，这有可能。但关于 alpha，人人都有权持有自己的观点。

turns.en: We're kind of more alpha skeptical, you know, I mean, that's why we're invested in broad index funds for our clients so much. So we're like alpha skeptics in general anyway.
turns.zh: 我们在 alpha 上偏怀疑。这就是为什么我们客户的钱大量放在宽基指数基金里。我们本来就是广义上的 alpha 怀疑论者。

turns.en: So why the hype around the products? People love to pay less taxes. I mean, I think some people would like rather pay somebody a fee and pay less taxes and be in the same place than not paying the fee and paying more taxes.
turns.zh: 那为什么这类产品被炒得这么热？人们就是爱少缴税。我是说，有些人宁愿付给别人一笔费用、少缴点税，即使最终结果差不多，也好过不付费用、多缴税。

turns.en: And you know, I think that some of the purveyors analyze the tax benefits in a fairly optimistic way, you know, like maybe, oh, you're going to roll this until forever and then you're going to get step up in basis or we're going to do a 351 into an ETF.
turns.zh: 而且我觉得，有些卖方对税收收益的分析相当乐观，比如：这个可以一直滚动下去，最后你会拿到成本基础的提升（step-up in basis），或者我们会用 Section 351 把它转入一只 ETF。

turns.en: I don't know how people are marketing it, but if you're an RIA, you're like, hey, I've got this great thing for you client, you know, I'm charging you some money to be your RIA.
turns.zh: 我不知道大家是怎么做营销的。但如果你是 RIA，你可能会说：嘿，我有一个特别棒的东西给你，客户，我收你一点费用当你的 RIA，

turns.en: Here's this shiny new thing, you know, people like shiny new things. This is not even close to the weirdest things going on in our marketplace today.
turns.zh: 来，这是个闪亮的新玩具。人们就是爱闪亮的新东西。这甚至都远不算我们市场上今天最怪异的事。

turns.en: Like we should be saying, why are people buying these buffer funds? You know, it's like the things of why are people doing X? This is like, I've got one for buffer funds.
turns.zh: 我们更该问的是：为什么人们要买那些缓冲型基金（buffer funds）？就像，为什么大家要做 X？这个我有一个关于 buffer funds 的吐槽。

turns.en: This is like almost defensible. This is in the zone of defensible. Like we're saying, eh, it's not quite worth it on a risk adjusted basis. Like we're not saying it's terrible.
turns.zh: 多空税损收割这个几乎还算站得住，在还能辩护的范围内。我们是说：嗯，从风险调整后的角度看不太值。我们不是糟透它。

turns.en: There's other stuff that's terrible on your perspective on this. You guys do run an ETF, but you've got clients like effectively wealth management type clients.
turns.zh: 按你的观点还有更糟的。你们自己也管着一只 ETF，但你们也有那种财富管理客户。

turns.en: And so you come to something like this from the perspective of let's do the research and see if we should be using it. Is that the right way to characterize it?
turns.zh: 所以你看待这类东西的方式是：先做研究，看我们该不该用它。这样描述对吗？

turns.en: Well we actually built a direct index tax loss harvesting product and we ran it on some of our own money for a couple of years and we were just thinking about it because people were asking us to do it and we built it.
turns.zh: 其实我们真的做过一个直接指数化税损收割产品，拿我们自己的钱跑了两三年。当时因为有人要求我们做，我们就做了，顺便想了想。

turns.en: We thought it was a good version of it and we're like, ugh, we don't want to offer this to clients. Other clients get about the same amount of expected tax losses or a tax efficiency, but keep it simple and not get into this whole thing.
turns.zh: 我们本来觉得那是个不错的版本，结果我们说：呃，我们不想把这个卖给客户。其他客户用简单方法得到的预期税收亏损或税务效率差不多，就别再卷进这一大摊子里。

turns.en: I mean, one of the big problems with direct index tax loss harvesting is that always in the back of your mind, you're going to be wondering, everybody knows kind of what these direct index tax loss harvesters trades are going to be.
turns.zh: 直接指数化税损收割的一大问题是：你心底永远在犯嘀咕。因为所有人都多少知道这些直接指数化税损收割者会做什么交易。

turns.en: IBM is down. Somebody's going to harvest that. Everybody's going to harvest that. And there's a trillion dollars in these programs. And we're wondering about, how is Jane Street and Citadel and Rentec and all these guys, how are they making money every single day of the year without ever losing money in general?
turns.zh: IBM 跌了，肯定有人要收割这笔亏损。所有人都要去收割它。这些项目里躺着一万亿美元。我们一直在琢磨：Jane Street、Citadel、RenTech 这些公司，是怎么做到一年三百六十五天每天都在赚钱、而且总体上从不亏钱的？

turns.en: Not quite these days, but close. That might well be part of it when Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan are making billions of dollars on their trading dust.
turns.zh: 最近不全是这样了，但很接近。当 Goldman Sachs 和 JPMorgan 在它们的交易台上一年赚几十亿的时候，这很可能就是其中一部分。

turns.en: So you've got to wonder and throw in their millennium and Bally Astley and all these guys. If you start to underperform in your direct index tax loss harvesting thing, if you're underperforming, you're going to be like, oh, this is terrible.
turns.zh: 所以你得琢磨，还得算上 Millennium、Balyasny，所有这些家伙。如果你的直接指数化税损收割组合开始跑输——你跑输了，你会说：

turns.en: This is what's happening. And you're going to be really bothered by it. And if you're outperforming, you're going to be like, oh, I got lucky.
turns.zh: 太可怕了，这就是正在发生的事，你会非常难受。而如果你跑赢了，你会说：哦，我运气好。

turns.en: You know that the direct index tax loss harvesting guys are not doing any analysis. They're just trying to do the tax loss harvesting and manage the tracking error.
turns.zh: 你知道那些直接指数化税损收割公司并没有做任何投资分析，他们只想完成税损收割、把跟踪误差管住。

turns.en: So when it goes well, it's like, oh, this is great. I got lucky. When it goes badly, it's like, oh, I got picked off by Citadel. That's interesting.
turns.zh: 所以顺的时候你说：哇，真棒，我运气好。不顺的时候你说：哦，我被 Citadel 收割了。这就有意思了。

turns.en: And that's uncomfortable. And that's like a big reason that we just thought, oh, this is so uncomfortable. If you're really reporting your returns properly to investors, it's just going to be super uncomfortable to be saying, oh, you underperformed by 75 basis points and we don't know why.
turns.zh: 那种感觉很不安。那也是我们最终决定不做的大原因：太不舒服了。如果你真的在向投资人如实报告收益，你就得不停地说：你跑输了 75 个基点，我们不知道为什么，

turns.en: It was just bad luck. And then it's like, oh gosh, I don't want to do that. Yeah. The tracking error, the comment about maybe the tax loss harvesting trades are priced in and so you're given up whatever tax benefit there might be to asset pricing when you trade.
turns.zh: 纯属倒霉。天哪，这种日子我不想过。是啊。关于跟踪误差，你之前提到，也许税损收割的交易已经被定价进去了，所以那点税收好处在交易时就被资产定价吃掉了。

turns.en: Yeah. A little bit of frictions. I mean, we know trading has frictions and when a lot of people are doing the same thing, it has impact. But I don't know.
turns.zh: 是有一点。有一点摩擦成本。我是说，我们知道交易有摩擦，当很多人做同样的交易时，就有冲击。但我不清楚。

turns.en: We've never done any research on that. It's just a hypothesis, a speculative hypothesis. We like simplicity too. When your research and analysis supports the simple answer, we're always excited to see that.
turns.zh: 那个我们没做过研究。只是一个假说，推测性的假说。我们也喜欢简单。当你的研究和分析支持那个简单的答案时，我们总是看到就很高兴。

turns.en: Yeah, definitely. Why isn't a crystal ball enough to beat the market? This is one of our favorite bits of research that we did. It kind of sat with us for a long time.
turns.zh: 对，太有意思了。为什么水晶球都不足以战胜市场？这是我们最喜欢的自研项目之一。这个点子跟我们搁了很久。

turns.en: We did this research where we wanted to test out something that Nassim Taleb had tweeted about long ago. He said, give a man the front page of the Wall Street Journal a day ahead of time every day of the year and within a year, he'll be broke.
turns.zh: 我们做了这个研究，想验证 Nassim Taleb 很多年前发的一条推文。他说：每天提前一天，把次日的《华尔街日报》头版给一个人看，一年之内，他就会破产。

turns.en: It's like, wow, that would be so interesting to try to test this out. We created a game where we give people the front page of the Wall Street Journal a day ahead historically and let them trade on that in stocks and bonds and see how they do.
turns.zh: 我们就想：哇，要能验证这个就太酷了。我们做了一个游戏，把历史上提前一天的《华尔街日报》头版给人看，让他们据此交易股票和债券，看结果如何。

turns.en: A lot of those days are employment days and Fed announcement days, so there's real news. We ran the experiment with real money, mostly with MBA and finance graduate students to begin with and some practitioners, and then we just opened it up.
turns.zh: 那些日子里很多是就业数据发布日和美联储公告日，所以是有真实新闻的。我们一开始用真金白银做实验，主要找 MBA 和金融专业研究生，还有一些从业者，然后就把游戏向所有人开放了。

turns.en: We've had 100,000 people or more play it since then for fun. It's really hard to generate a good return. Turns out that on average, people didn't do very well despite having this newspaper a full day ahead of time.
turns.zh: 从那以后有超过十万人玩过这个游戏，纯属娱乐。要做出好回报真的很难。结果是，平均而言，尽管提前一整天看到报纸，大家做得并不好。

turns.en: Part of it, I think there are two things mostly going on or three things maybe. One of them is people really had a hard time sizing their bets in a sensible way.
turns.zh: 一部分原因——我想主要有两三个原因。第一，人们真的很难给下注规模一个合理的分配。

turns.en: People oversized their bets. They were sure that stocks were going to go up because they could use leverage in our experiment. They would be like 40 times leveraged and the market would go down 2%.
turns.zh: 人们把注押得太重。他们确信股票会涨，因为我们的实验里可以用杠杆，他们敢上 40 倍杠杆，结果市场跌 2%。

turns.en: That was it. They lost 80% on that day and they couldn't come back from that. One is that the sizing just didn't correspond to sensible sizing or proportional to how clear the signals were.
turns.zh: 就这样，那一天就亏 80%，再也翻不了身。一个问题是，仓位大小跟合理规模对不上，没有和信号的清晰程度成比例。

turns.en: Sometimes the signals were pretty clear and other times not, and people didn't size like that so much. That was one thing. Many of the people who played the game really wanted to trade stocks, but the news is much more economic and Wall Street Journal news is much less ambiguous when it comes to bonds.
turns.zh: 有时候信号相当清晰，有时候并不，而人们并没有按信号的清晰度来定仓位，这是一方面。很多玩这个游戏的人特别想交易股票，但新闻大多偏宏观，而《华尔街日报》的新闻在债券上其实模糊性小得多。

turns.en: When you get something that's like the economy is stronger than we thought, well, that could be good for stocks or that could be bad for stocks because interest rates might be going up, but it's bad for bonds generally.
turns.zh: 当新闻说经济比我们想的更强，这对股票可能好也可能坏，因为利率可能要升。但对债券，一般来说都是坏的。

turns.en: We also found that people had a predilection to speculate in stocks more than bonds and they would have done better in the bonds in general.
turns.zh: 我们还发现，人们就是偏爱投机股票而不是债券，而总体上他们做债券其实会更好。

turns.en: People did better in their guesses on bonds. Then people just had some difficulty parsing the news. When we brought in some senior macro type traders to play, we got six or seven of those guys to play it and they did well, but they only had a hit ratio of like 60%, but still they did well.
turns.zh: 人们对债券方向的判断准确率更高。然后，人们在解读新闻上也有些困难。当我们请来一些资深的宏观交易员来玩——我们找了六七个——他们做得不错，但命中率也就 60% 左右，可即便如此他们还是赚得好。

turns.en: They had a good sharp ratio in the end after 15 things and they doubled their money on average over 15 sets of bets. So it was possible to do well.
turns.zh: 下了 15 注之后，他们最终的夏普比率不错，平均在 15 注里把钱翻了一倍。所以这是可以做得好的。

turns.en: Quite a lot of experience was needed. I think if you gave the front page a day ahead of time to a bunch of macro traders, they would make good money over time.
turns.zh: 需要相当多的经验。我想如果把提前一天的头版给一帮宏观交易员，他们长期能赚到不错的钱。

turns.en: They wouldn't be making their money grow tenfold. They doubled their money after 15 of these. Those were some of the interesting findings and then of course, I think you'll probably ask, we had this idea like a year later to let the AIs loose on it and to let the AIs play and that was as much fun as anything.
turns.zh: 但他们也不是让钱翻十倍。他们是在 15 注之后翻一倍。这些都是有意思的发现。然后，你肯定也会问到的：大约一年后，我们想到让 AI 也来放开玩，让 AI 来下注，那本身就乐趣无穷。

turns.en: Once you brought it up, I was going to ask about it. Yeah, you have to. How did the AIs perform relative to the humans? We got the AIs to play and we'd spent a lot of time trying to make sure that they weren't like cheating, like figuring out, oh, that front page was from this date and figuring out what happened exactly on that date.
turns.zh: 你一提起，我正想问这个。对，必须问。AI 相对人类表现如何？我们让 AI 来玩。我们花了很多时间确保它们没有作弊——比如发现这张头版是哪一天的、然后去查那天到底发生了什么。

turns.en: So we're pretty sure that they didn't do that. And we're also pretty sure they didn't do that because the first time that we let them loose on it, they didn't do very well.
turns.zh: 我们相当确定它们没这么干。而且我们也相当确定它们没有，因为我们第一次放开让它们玩的时候，它们做得并不好。

turns.en: They had a good hit ratio, but they took too much risk. They didn't size things correctly. Now we were using the free versions and this is what six months ago or so, so we were using free versions as of six months ago.
turns.zh: 它们命中率不错，但冒险太多，仓位大小没调对。注意，我们当时用的是免费版本——大概是六个月前——用的是大约六个月前的免费版。

turns.en: We weren't using Fable. When we then went for the paid versions of three of them, because we couldn't get a paid version of Grock going, the paid versions of Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini did better than the more free versions.
turns.zh: 我们没用 Fable。后来我们去买了其中三家的付费版——因为 Grok 的付费版我们没能跑起来——Claude、ChatGPT 和 Gemini 的付费版都比免费版好。

turns.en: And then when we told the AIs to read our book, The Missing Billionaires and to think more about sizing, then they did even better. They probably became a little bit overly conservative, but they did a really good job on figuring out whether the markets would go up or down and how strong.
turns.zh: 然后我们让 AI 先读我们的书《Missing Billionaires》、更多思考仓位规模的问题，它们就做得更好了。它们可能变得有点过于保守，但对市场涨跌方向的判断和强弱把握真的很好。

turns.en: I mean, they were smart. It was impressive, but they got the sizing wrong to begin with, which was interesting. If we probably did it today, they'd probably do better because the non-premium versions are probably much better than the best versions were back then, but it was really interesting to see that generation of AIs play the game and do well, except also struggle with sizing a bit.
turns.zh: 我是说，它们很聪明，令人印象深刻。但一开始它们搞错了仓位大小，这很有意思。如果我们今天再做一遍，它们可能表现更好，因为现在的非付费版本可能就已经比当时最好的版本强多了。但看着那一代 AI 玩这个游戏、做得不错、又在仓位规模上挣扎，真的很有意思。

turns.en: How much attention do you think normal investors should pay to the news? In terms of investing, very little. In terms of human experience, in terms of our life as humans, I think it's important to know what's going on in the world to be good citizens and all of that.
turns.zh: 普通投资者在投资上应该花多少注意力看新闻？在投资层面，非常少。在人生体验层面，作为人，我觉得了解世界在发生什么、做个合格公民，这些很重要。

turns.en: But I think as an investor, close to zero. I think as an investor, you just don't need to be following the news very much at all. I think that a sensible long-term investing strategy, even if it's a dynamic asset allocation variety, just doesn't really need to follow the news very much at all, very little.
turns.zh: 但作为投资者，我觉得几乎为零。我觉得作为一个投资者，你根本不太需要去盯新闻。我觉得一个明智的长期投资策略——哪怕是动态资产配置那种——其实都不太需要跟着新闻走，几乎不需要。

turns.en: I think that as people, though, we have a responsibility to follow it somewhat. Got to be informed to some extent. Isn't it just amazing? Even when we're following the news, just how little we are really seeing of what's going on in the world.
turns.zh: 但作为人，我们有责任多少跟进一下，得有一定程度的知情。是不是很神奇？就算我们一直在看新闻，我们真正看到的世界上正在发生的事，其实少得可怜。

turns.en: I don't even know the last time that I heard about what's happening in Thailand. No idea. Every once in a while, it's like, this happened in South Africa or this happened in India.
turns.zh: 我甚至不记得上次听到泰国在发生什么是什么时候了。完全不知道。偶尔听说一下，南非出了这事，印度出了那事。

turns.en: We get such a narrow version of news and I don't know what we could do about it because there's just so much news. How much of it could we consume anyway?
turns.zh: 我们拿到的新闻是一个非常狭窄的版本。我也不知道我们能怎么办，因为新闻实在太多，我们又能消化多少呢？

turns.en: That's an interesting question. Not all of it, probably. Yeah. How do you choose? How concerning do you think the amount of leverage in the US stock market is currently?
turns.zh: 这倒是个有意思的问题。总之消化不了全部。是啊，你怎么筛选？你现在怎么看美国股市杠杆的规模，有多令人担忧？

turns.en: Leverage is something that we built into our model for who killed the random walk paper and then we didn't wind up using it at all. We kind of left it out even though we built that in.
turns.zh: 杠杆是我们为 Who Killed the Random Walk 那篇论文建模型时做进去的，但最后我们根本没用上，虽然我们把杠杆搭进去了。

turns.en: But leverage certainly exacerbates all of the instabilities that we have. I think that the leverage is concerning, particularly the leverage that we have embedded in leveraged ETFs, which we know have to do systematic trades at the end of every day where when the market or stock or whatever the thing is based on goes down, they have to sell and when it goes up, they have to buy.
turns.zh: 但杠杆确实会放大我们所有的不稳定因素。我认为杠杆是值得担忧的，尤其是埋在杠杆 ETF 里的那种。我们知道这些产品必须在每天收盘时做系统性交易：当它跟踪的股票或标的下跌时，它们必须卖出；上涨时，它们必须买入。

turns.en: Margin interest is pretty big, but I don't think margin interest is terribly concerning. It probably helps that Fidelity and Schwab are still charging 9% for margin, and so I think that makes it clear to many people that you don't want to be running leverage longs for long.
turns.zh: 保证金利息的规模相当大，但我不认为 margin 本身有多可怕。有一个原因可能还好：Fidelity 和 Schwab 的保证金利率还是 9%，所以我想这至少让很多人清楚，你不该长期跑杠杆多头。

turns.en: Then we have this absolute explosion in options trading. That is effectively potentially a lot of leverage. When you go back and think about October of 1987, that Black Monday and how the Brady Commission or whatever was like, yeah, this got caused by portfolio insurance and the trades that needed to be done and the portfolio insurers need to sell 60 billion of stocks and that set the whole thing off.
turns.zh: 然后就是期权交易的彻底爆发，这实际上是潜在的巨大杠杆。回想 1987 年 10 月那个黑色星期一（Black Monday），Brady 委员会当时说：是的，这件事是组合保险（portfolio insurance）造成的，是那些必须做的交易——组合保险策略需要卖出 600 亿美元的股票——整个事情就这么引爆了。

turns.en: I think that the market can absorb things sometimes and other times it doesn't. I think the leverage is concerning, not massively concerning, but concerning.
turns.zh: 我觉得市场有时能消化这些东西，有时消化不了。我认为杠杆是令人担忧的，不是极度担忧，但令人担忧。

turns.en: There's more than meets the eye from just looking at the margin figures. All of a sudden, you hear about something like the situational awareness situation.
turns.zh: 光看 margin 数字，水面下的东西比看到的要多。突然你就听到某个东西，比如 Situational Awareness 那档子事。

turns.en: I never knew about that lever. I had no idea who else is out there with leverage and leverage long shorts. Fidelity and Schwab are saying, hey, going back to the leverage long short direct index thing, they're saying, we're a little bit concerned about this.
turns.zh: 我之前完全不知道那个层面的情况。也不知道还有谁在用杠杆、用加杠杆的多空。回到杠杆多空直接指数化这事：Fidelity 和 Schwab 在说：我们对此有点担心。

turns.en: We don't want too much more of this on our custodial balance sheet or in our custodial system because they're a little bit worried about it.
turns.zh: 我们不想让太多这种东西出现在我们的托管资产负债表上、进入我们的托管系统，因为他们有点担心。

turns.en: The markets can really deal with a certain amount of leverage, but that same amount of leverage sometimes can be problematic. Situational awareness, just for any listeners who don't follow the financial news as closely as we do, was a fund that was highly levered, invested in AI related stocks and had a fabulously large downfall or decline in the value of its holdings.
turns.zh: 市场确实能消化一定量的杠杆，但同样量的杠杆，有时候就是会出问题。Situational Awareness——给不常盯财经新闻的听众解释一下——那是一支高杠杆的基金，投的是 AI 相关的股票，然后它的持仓价值出现了戏剧性的大跌。

turns.en: Yeah, I guess not downfall, but decline, yeah, and there's like a lot of leverage that we didn't know about. I know listeners will have caught on to the comment about the daily resets on leverage ETFs because we've had some discussion within our podcast community about how, from the investor's perspective, daily resets are actually not a terrible thing, even for a long term investor, but you're talking about the effect, I think, on volatility and asset prices in
turns.zh: 嗯，我想 downfall 这个词不对，应该是下跌。是啊，有太多我们此前不知道的杠杆。听友们应该已经注意到我们提到杠杆 ETF 每日重置（daily reset）那句评论了，因为我们在自己的播客社区里讨论过：从投资者角度看，每日重置其实并不是坏事，即便是长期投资者也无妨。但你谈的应该是它对市场波动和资产价格的影响。

turns.en: the market. There is a recent paper looking at the effect of leverage ETFs on the Korean stock market recently and they do show that in that case, it's a smaller market, obviously different environment than the US, but they did significantly increase volatility, which is pretty interesting.
turns.zh: 最近有一篇论文看的是杠杆 ETF 对韩国股市的影响。他们确实发现，在那个案例里——韩国市场显然更小，环境和美国不同——杠杆 ETF 显著推高了波动率，这很有意思。

turns.en: Boy, that Korean market, that's incredible, yeah. Things spill over. There's all kinds of interrelationships, which is all pretty highly nonlinear, all this stuff.
turns.zh: 哇，韩国那个市场，太惊人了。是啊，风险是会传染外溢的。这些东西之间有各种相互关联，而这一切都是高度非线性的。

turns.en: We have the butterfly effects where like a small thing can really get things going with these interrelationships. So when does it make sense to borrow to invest in stocks or any other risky assets?
turns.zh: 我们有蝴蝶效应：一件小事，通过这些相互关联，就可能把整个局面带动起来。那什么时候借钱投资股票或其他风险资产是有道理的？

turns.en: So first of all, the iconic, sensible case for leverage involves young people where they have a lot of human capital, where hopefully a lot of that human capital is not highly related to the stock market.
turns.zh: 首先，最经典、最合理的杠杆情形是年轻人：他们有大量人力资本（human capital），而且希望这部分人力资本和股市的相关性不太高。

turns.en: So they have human capital and it doesn't have a super high beta, so to speak. And they don't have much financial capital and they're like, okay, well, how much stock should I own?
turns.zh: 就是他们的人力资本 beta 没有那么高。而他们的金融资本不多。那他们就想：好，我该持有多少股票呢？

turns.en: They're like, well, I should own 50% of my total wealth, my financial capital, my human capital in the stock market. And it's like, well, I just have a little bit of financial capital, so I should be leveraged.
turns.zh: 他们应该把全部财富——金融资本加人力资本——的 50% 放在股市里。可我的金融资本这么一点，所以我该上杠杆。

turns.en: This makes rational sense. The problem though with it is that leverage is expensive in general. It's also, the leverage is pretty variable in terms of cost, but we talked just a moment ago about Fidelity and Schwab, E-Trade, I don't know, I mean every brokerage sort of has their own cost of leverage, which tends to be on average really high for offering leverage through brokerage accounts.
turns.zh: 这在理性上说得通。但问题在于：一般来说杠杆很贵，而且杠杆成本波动也大。我们刚才才聊到 Fidelity、Schwab、E-Trade——我不知道，每家券商的杠杆成本都不同，而通过券商账户加杠杆的平均成本真的很高。

turns.en: There are a few places that have lower costs of leverage and also sometimes futures are implicitly giving you leverage at a lower cost than those high costs of 9% or whatever at Fidelity and Schwab.
turns.zh: 有少数地方的杠杆成本低一些。有时候期货也隐含地给你提供了比 9% 低得多的杠杆成本。

turns.en: But it's hard to be an individual investor and to be borrowing at less than 1% over Treasury bills or 1.5% over Treasury bills. That's the very best that you can do on relatively small size, which is kind of the case of the person who doesn't have much financial capital.
turns.zh: 但对个人投资者来说，想在国库券利率之上只加 1%、1.5% 借钱，几乎做不到。这已经是在相对小额度下最好的水平了，而恰恰就是金融资本不多的人面对的处境。

turns.en: That person doesn't have $50 million to have it interactive brokers and get the overnight rate plus 50 basis points. That person is going to be at 1.5% over the overnight rate.
turns.zh: 那个人没有 5000 万美元，放到 Interactive Brokers 上过隔夜利率加 50 个基点。那个人拿到的是隔夜利率加 1.5%。

turns.en: And so now it becomes a question of, well, if the expected return of stocks is just 2 or 3% higher than the risk-free rate, does it really make sense to borrow paying 1.5% because that 1.5% is a sure cost.
turns.zh: 于是问题变成：如果股票的预期回报只比无风险利率高 2% 到 3%，那么付出 1.5% 这个确定的成本去借钱，真的合算吗？

turns.en: The 3% is a risky expected return and we need to kind of haircut that to make it risk-adjusted. There just tends to not be a lot of juice there, depends a little bit on the environment.
turns.zh: 那 3% 是有风险的预期回报，我们得打个折扣把它风险调整一下。所以这里面往往没多少油水，具体也要看环境。

turns.en: Right now we're in a low expected return environment. Levering up probably doesn't make sense for most people. It could make some sense for some people, but in general we'd say it probably isn't worth the complexity, the risk of losing most of your savings.
turns.zh: 现在我们在一个低预期回报的环境里。对大多数人来说，加杠杆大概并不合理。对某些人也许有点道理，但总体上我们会说：不值得去承担这份复杂性和输掉大半积蓄的风险。

turns.en: It kind of hurts. You're 27 years old and you saved up a couple hundred thousand dollars and all of a sudden you have $30,000 left because you were leveraged doing something sensible, but still that pain is tough and you need to be monitoring it and keeping the exposure constant and all of that.
turns.zh: 那真的很痛。你 27 岁，攒了大约二十万美元，结果突然只剩三万美元，因为你在做一件理性的事——加杠杆——但那种痛就是难受。你还得时刻盯盘、保持敞口恒定，诸如此类。

turns.en: So in some places the deleveraging happens automatically. You don't get a chance to make a margin call to top up or to do it yourself. We would say that for older people that have a lot of financial capital relative to their human capital, probably it doesn't make sense to leverage and for younger people it's more of a borderline call and maybe just keeping things simpler and not doing it makes sense
turns.zh: 有些地方的去杠杆是自动发生的，你根本不会有补保证金的机会，也不会轮到自己处理。我们会说：对老年人来说，金融资本相对于人力资本已经很多，加杠杆大概没道理；对年轻人来说，这是个模棱两可的决定，也许保持简单、不加杠杆才是对的，

turns.en: and just focusing on getting the savings into the market is going to be more comfortable. Spent a lot of time recently reading about leveraged ETFs, like just long leveraged index ETFs.
turns.zh: 专心把储蓄投进市场会更舒服。我最近花了大量时间读杠杆 ETF 的东西，就是纯做多的指数杠杆 ETF。

turns.en: The spreads above the risk free rate are around 50 basis points, which is not crazy, but of course you're paying the 1% or whatever it is or 80 basis point fee to get access to that.
turns.zh: 它们相对无风险利率的利差大约 50 个基点，这个不算离谱，当然你要付那个 1%、或者 80 个基点的费用才能拿到。

turns.en: It's not really that cheap, but it's maybe better than margin rates at brokerages. You do have non-re... It's certainly better than Fidelity or Schwab, but I mean it starts to look like going long futures.
turns.zh: 这并不算便宜，但可能比券商的保证金利率好。当然，跟做多期货差不多。

turns.en: In the product it's closer to that. The thing that I realized looking at these over the last kind of couple of months is that the live history of the US equity leveraged ETFs has been through a period of time where interest rates were super low and equity returns have been super high and so people look at these products and they're like, wow, I want to leave her up because look how good the returns are.
turns.zh: 在产品结构上它确实更接近期货。我这两个月研究这些产品最大的感触是：美国股票类杠杆 ETF 的整个实盘历史，恰好覆盖了利率超低、股票回报超高的时期。所以人们看这些产品就说：哇，我要加杠杆，你看回报多好。
